title: Coercive Control
description: A systematic pattern of domination using threats, intimidation, isolation, micromanagement, and degradation to strip a person of autonomy and agency.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: A systematic pattern of domination that goes beyond physical violence, using threats, intimidation, isolation, micromanagement, and degradation to strip a person of autonomy and agency.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A partner monitors your movements via GPS, dictates what you wear, and controls finances so you have no independent money.
A parent makes all decisions for an adult child, including career, partners, and daily schedule, using guilt and threats of disownment.
A manager controls not just your work but your lunch breaks, bathroom timing, and personal interactions, enforcing absurd rules with humiliation.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Surveillance: checking phones, emails, location.
Regulation: setting rules for appearance, speech, and daily activities.
Deprivation: restricting access to money, food, or sleep.
Degradation: constant belittling to destroy self-worth.
Threat: implied or explicit danger to self, loved ones, or pets.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “I do this because I love you.”
“You’d be lost without me.”
“If you leave, I’ll make sure everyone knows what you really are.”
“No one else would put up with you.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You need permission for normal activities.
You’ve lost access to your own bank account or your spending is monitored.
You feel more like property than a partner, child, or employee.
Your decisions are pre-made; you’re just executing them.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Coercive control works by eroding the victim’s sense of self-efficacy and reality. Learned helplessness sets in; the victim internalizes the controller’s voice. It is a liberty crime that can precede lethal outcomes.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Recognize that control is not love. Love expands freedom; control shrinks it.
Maintain independent resources: secret bank account, important documents stored safely, a code word with a friend.
If you suspect you’re in a coercive control situation, reach out to a specialized domestic abuse service.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Thinking coercive control is less serious than physical violence. It often causes deeper psychological harm and is a predictor of future lethality.
Believing you can reason with a controller. The goal isn’t a fair discussion; it’s compliance.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A husband gradually takes over all household finances, gives his wife an allowance, monitors her phone, and criticizes any outing with friends. She stops seeing people because the conflict isn’t worth it. Years later, she realizes she hasn’t made a single independent decision in a decade. She doesn’t know her own bank’s phone number.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: A cage doesn’t need bars. It can be built from criticism, surveillance, and guilt—invisible, but just as imprisoning.
